reason: B is easier to follow because of its explicit state machine (A_ACTIVE, FENCING, B_PROMOTED, B_ACTIVE), its trigger table and its failure table keyed by state, which show plainly what starts each step, where state lives and how resume works, while A spreads the same mechanics across dense prose with many nested caveats.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the central mechanism (the external record, the lease-based self-fence and the parallel branches after promotion) up front and compactly, then puts triggers and failure handling into two scannable tables; B covers the same ground in longer, denser prose and leaves more open questions, so a newcomer would take longer to get the core flow from it.

author: sonnet

author: sonnet
reason: A sets out the setup, components, the active-region record and the step sequence in a cleaner order, and its diagram shows the failure branches, so a newcomer sees what happens faster; B packs more detail and timings into longer steps and its diagram leaves out the branches.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a short version, explains its few terms in plain language and gives a clean, linear diagram and a timer walkthrough, so an outsider sees the flow quickly; A is more exhaustive but buries the flow under about 30 glossary terms, heavily nested diagram branches and a long failure table.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the mechanism with fewer moving parts: one locked transaction per tick, an outbox, and timer rows. author: haiku
reason: A states each trigger, the single owner of each write, where state lives and each failure case in one consistent way, while B contradicts itself: the evaluator writes in one place and the incident manager in another, streaks sit on incidents that don't exist yet, and a page_log row is "one per attempt" yet keyed uniquely on (incident, level).

author: haiku
reason: B says exactly what starts each step (the evaluator calls the incident manager after its commit, timers carry a level, acks share the same row lock), keeps its rules consistent and puts every failure in one scannable table, while A's diagram treats the primary page and escalation pages differently (it logs after sending in one case and claims before sending in the other) and leaves the sweep and crash behaviour harder to work out.

author: sonnet

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the same mechanism in less space: the state lives in three tables, each step is claimed with an insert or a compare-and-set, and failures are grouped in one list, while B's opening overview is good but its sprawling diagram branches, six tables and long failure table give the reader more to untangle.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to follow: its sequence diagram is split into labelled phases with alt branches, all timers are plain Postgres rows with fixed due times, and state, coordination, timers and failures each get their own section, while A packs many edge cases into each step and uses a less intuitive order (queue the timer before inserting the incident, timers that are never cancelled).

author: sonnet
reason: A describes each step clearly: its sequence diagram is split into labelled phases with explicit branches, and separate sections cover where state lives, how the two instances coordinate, how the timers work and what happens on failure. B's flat diagram has no branches and an unintuitive order (timer queued before the incident is inserted), and it leaves unclear how its separate incident manager is deployed.

author: haiku
reason: B is quicker to follow and harder to misread: it sets out the refund states, the allowed transitions and the tables before the steps, and it gives each background job its own state to work on (the sweeper handles `queued`, the reconciler handles `pending`); A puts several sub-states inside `pending`, which the reader has to rebuild from `attempts` and `provider_refund_id`, and its reconciliation step uses three age-based branches.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow for three reasons: it opens with a short map of which steps run in the admin's request, which run in the background worker, and which record the result; it uses a simpler state model where only `pending` can change; and it ends with a summary of failure handling across all steps, whereas A makes the reader keep five states, a queue, a sweeper, a reconciler and the 23-hour rules in mind.
